We thank the reviewer for their additional comments and would like to clarify the mentioned points as follows.

> Regarding cross-section parts, I did not think the method was more explicit than the other ones. The main differences lie in the raster image-based sketch prediction, and the method still requires an image encoder to implicitly estimate the sketch parameters. Personally, I did not treat it as a very significant difference, especially since raster images are just the intermediate results for feature encoding and there are not very specific network designs
> 

We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s assessment of the proposed "explicit modeling". Our approach **explicitly** introduces a three-step reverse engineering pipeline. This allows to focus on the individual stages separately, hence reducing the solution space for each stage. This is clearly different from [a,b] where the methods are implicitly conditioned on subsets of point clouds. The results reported in Table 1 (Quantitative Results on Complex Models) and Figure 4 (fine-grained geometric details) demonstrate the value of the proposed explicit modeling for recovering fine-grained geometrical details in CAD reconstruction.

> Regarding the constraints, I also thought the contribution of sketch constraints was unclear. It simply adds an additional task that predicts sketch constraints, and I did not find interesting designs or insights, despite its importance to CAD reconstructions.
> 

The interest in the proposed explicit modeling of the reverse engineering pipeline lies in enabling sketch constraint inference directly from rasterized images. This significantly reduces the solution space compared to predicting constraints from point clouds. This strategy should not be seen as simply adding an extra task. It is actually key in enabling the inference of sketch constraints **for the first time in 3D reverse engineering literature**. Moreover, the experiments in Section 5.2, inspired by designer practices, clearly demonstrate the value of constraints in enhancing **CAD model editability**. We believe these findings are very relevant insights for future 3D reverse engineering research.

> For the invisible extrusions, I did not get how the method can handle it. I agreed that a reconstruction does not need to replicate the original construction history, but there needs to be a way to predict sketches for subtracted extrusions. The results show the method outperforms CAD-SIGNET. However, this may be because of better extrusion parameters, and I did not find how this was related to invisible parts. Moreover, maybe all the mentioned methods have such limitations in representing sketches of subtracted extrusions.
> 

Cut extrusions can be categorized into: (1) *visible cut extrusions*, when their originating sketch loops are visible and nested within other loops; (2) *invisible cut extrusions*, when their sketch loops are invisible in the final CAD geometry hence not captured by cross-sections. Our method handles *visible cut extrusions* as detailed in lines 221–225. The *invisible cut extrusions* are not directly handled. In such cases, the models are reverse engineered using alternative sketch–extrude sequences. As the reviewer noted, **other methods share the same limitation**. The experiment presented in the rebuttal demonstrates that our method outperforms CAD-SIGNet in reconstructing models with visible and invisible cut extrusions. Visual illustrations of individual reconstruction steps with both visible and invisible cut extrusions will be added in the paper (NeurIPS guidelines did not allow their inclusion in the rebuttal).

rebuttal.value:
## Contribution and cross-sections 

**Contribution:** The primary goal of MiCADangelo is to predict CAD sequences from 3D scans with *fine-grained details*. These sequences should be *seamlessly integrable* into CAD software, enabling *design-intent-aware editability through the inferred constraints*. To achieve this, MiCADangelo mimics the process typically followed by human designers when reconstructing CAD models from scans. These steps consist of: 

1- selecting a 2D cross-section from the 3D scan, which is handled by a dedicated cross-section plane detection model, described in Section 4.2. 

2- parameterizing and constraining the sketch within the extracted cross-section. This is accomplished using a specialized, constraint-aware sketch parameterization model that operates at the image level (see Section 4.3). 

3- applying a CAD operation, such as extrusion, to the parameterized sketch in order to generate a solid. This is modeled using our differentiable extrusion optimization, detailed in Section 4.4.


We believe that **explicitly** modeling the steps of the reverse engineering process, as performed by human designers, and making thoughtful technical design choices for each stage, constitutes a valuable contribution. This approach can also serve as a foundation for future research, encouraging exploration of alternative methods and extensions to the proposed design choices at each stage.


**Cross-section in prior works:** While CAD-SIGNet [a] and PS-CAD [b] mentioned by the reviewer attempt to use a slightly similar concept to the introduced cross-sections in our work, they *do not* employ *explicit* cross-sectional slicing. Instead, they incorporate *implicit* mechanisms to condition sketch inference on a relevant subset of the input cloud. CAD-SIGNet [a] introduces a Sketch Instance Guided Attention module that predicts attention scores for vertices relevant to sketch token predictions. PS-CAD [b] uses RANSAC to detect planes within the point cloud and embeds the points lying on these planes. These embedded points are then used as prompts to condition the sketch/extrude decoder. MiCADangelo’s key advantage w.r.t to these works is in its *explicit* modeling of cross-sections and the reformulation of sketch parameterization, shifting from conditioning on subsets of point cloud vertices to operating on rasterized cross-sectional images. This allows for the use of an image-based model dedicated to sketch parameterization and constraint inference. We believe that this explicit modeling enables more accurate handling of fine-grained details, which remains a significant challenge for both CAD-SIGNet [a] (as shown in Table 1 of our paper) and PS-CAD [b] (as noted in the conclusion of their paper). Finally, the PlankAssembly [c] work mentioned by the reviewer focuses on converting 2D line drawings from 3 orthographic views into 3D CAD models made of only cuboids. While this is a valuable contribution, its connection to our work and the broader topic of CAD reverse engineering is less clear.

We thank the reviewer for suggesting these works and we will highlight their differences w.r.t our work in the revised version. 


**Cross sections cannot fully capture sketch information:** Indeed, as the reviewer mentions, the sketch of a cut feature may not be visible in any extracted cross-section. However, this does not prevent MiCADangelo from effectively reconstructing the CAD model. The key distinction is that MiCADangelo does not need to replicate the original construction history followed by the CAD designer. When a cut removes material, the remaining shape taken after the cut already contains the modified profile, so the necessary shape information is still present. A human designer performing manual reverse engineering would operate in a similar way, that is, by slicing the mesh, tracing the visible profiles, and building an alternative sequence of sketches and features that yields the same solid. MiCADangelo automates this reverse-engineering paradigm. Even though the reconstruction may use a different series of operations, the resulting model reconstructs the target CAD geometry. 

To further demonstrate MiCADangelo’s effectiveness on models including cuts, we report the performance of our method and that of CAD-SIGNet on a subset of models from DeepCAD that each contain at least one cut extrusion. The results are presented in the Table below. We observe that our method outperforms CAD-SIGNet on this partition.

| **Method** | **Mean CD** | **Median CD** | **IR** | **IoU** | **ECD** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAD-SIGNet [15] | 4.95 | 0.77 | 3.0 | 65.5 | 3.97 |
| Ours | 4.26 | 0.64 | 3.5 | 71.8 | 3.13 |


**Visual result illustrating how a complete reconstruction is decomposed into a set of sketch-extrusions:** We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and we will include a figure showcasing sequential sketch-extrusions (including cuts) in the revised version. As due to NeurIPS guidelines, we are unable to include additional figures in the rebuttal.


[a] Cad-signet, CVPR 2024.
[b] PS-CAD, ACM TOG 2025.
[c] Plankassembly, ICCV 2023.


## Sketch constraints 

**Modeling of sketch constraints is incremental:** We clarify that the novelty of this work is not in proposing a new constraint modeling approach. Instead, we are the first to integrate constraint prediction into 3D reverse engineering. By reformulating the problem as cross-section image parameterization, we operate in the image domain where sketch primitives and constraints can be inferred more easily and accurately, compared to the more challenging task of predicting them directly from point clouds. Notably, learning constrained sketch sequences directly from point clouds in a CAD-SIGNet-style framework would drastically expand the solution space, as the resulting sequences are significantly longer and more complex to model. This proposed formulation also enables us to leverage large-scale sketch datasets such as SketchGraphs as no suitable datasets exist for learning sketch constraints directly from point clouds. 

It is important to note, however, that unlike [d, e], we adopt a dedicated model that jointly learns both sketch primitive parameters and their constraints in a single forward pass, directly from rasterized sketch images. This design choice, inspired by [35], enables the model to leverage shared information between primitives and constraints.


**Sketch constraints for better sketch prediction:** We emphasize that CAD constraints in our framework are not introduced as a mechanism to boost sketch prediction. Existing methods in the CAD sketch literature do not use constraints to enhance parameterization performance [d,e]. Instead, CAD constraints are a fundamental aspect of CAD modeling as they dictate how an object responds to future CAD modifications. In the evaluation presented in section 5.2, we demonstrate the CAD models reconstructed with MiCADangelo closely follow the ground-truth under modification in contrast to the unconstrained sequences generated by CAD-SIGNet. Note that while constraints are not strictly necessary for sketch parameterization, it has been shown in [35] that jointly learning primitives and constraints can marginally improve prediction accuracy for both tasks by leveraging the shared information between them. Further investigation on improved sketch parameterization with constraints is left for future work.

## Differentiable extrusion

**Advantages of differentiable extrusion optimization over prior approaches:** We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Implicit function-based methods such as Point2Cyl [8] and SECAD-Net [18] predict SDFs, which can be robust for surface reconstruction but do not produce native geometric primitives like lines and arcs. This limits their editability and compatibility with downstream CAD workflows, which require parametric representations. For extrusions, these methods depend on point cloud segmentation or bounding box detection to estimate extrusion length, introducing dependencies and potential error propagation. We also note that the differentiable extrusion in SECAD-Net enables end-to-end supervision but does not directly optimize extrusion parameters. In contrast, our method explicitly optimizes the extrusion length, guided by local geometry around each sketch loop. Rather than relying on segmentation or bounding box detection, our method infers extrusion length directly from local geometry, avoiding error-prone intermediate stages. As requested by *Reviewer wdwr* regarding multi-step error accumulation, including the extrusion optimization stage, we compared our extrusion optimization method to that of Point2Cyl [8]. The results show that our approach produces more accurate extrusions. We thank the reviewer and will clarify this in the paper.


**Interference of different extrusions:** All extrusion parameters are optimized jointly across sketch loops and key cross-section planes. While joint optimization could introduce interactions between nearby or overlapping extrusions, in practice, we observe minimal interference due to the spatial separation of most sketch loops. We totally agree with the reviewer that this is one limitation of the proposed extrusion optimization. As future work, a penalty term can be incorporated into the loss function that discourages overlapping or conflicting extrusions. We thank the reviewer and we will add this in the limitations of the paper.

In this work, we focus on axis-aligned extrusions, as these are the types represented in the DeepCAD dataset. ## Effect of Sketch Constraints

Sketch constraints are a core component of CAD modeling, as they govern how a design adapts when modified. When designers apply constraints (e.g., orthogonality) to sketch primitives (e.g., two lines), any changes made to one primitive are automatically adjusted to preserve these relationships. For example, if the parameters of one line are modified, the other will update accordingly to maintain orthogonality. In a reverse engineering context, it is highly desirable not only to infer accurate CAD geometry from input scans but also to recover the underlying *design intent*, ensuring that the reconstructed model responds to modifications in a manner consistent with how a designer would have originally constrained it. This is exactly what the experiment conducted in Section 5.2 (results in Table 3 and Figure 5) is intended to show. Specifically, we applied identical random perturbations to the sketch primitives of both the ground-truth and the predicted CAD models—using our method and that of [15]—and evaluated the similarity of the resulting geometries with respect to the modified ground-truth. In the presence of constraints (e.g., orthogonality), perturbing one primitive (e.g., the endpoint of a line) can influence others (e.g., the parameters of the other line). If the constraints are correctly inferred, such modifications should propagate consistently across the geometry, resulting in similar outcomes. As shown in Table 3 and Figure 5, our method produces CAD geometries that closely match the perturbed ground-truth, demonstrating its ability to capture constraint-aware editability.

Taking another perspective, one can think that the learning of sketch constraints might have an effect on improving the sketch parameterization, hence the overall CAD reconstruction (e.g., inferring orthogonality constraint can help in enforcing the parameters of the predicted lines to be orthogonal). Prior work [35] has shown that at the sketch-level, jointly learning sketch parameterization and a constraint prediction similar to the one performed in MiCADangelo, can improve performance in both tasks due to shared information between them. We leave further exploration of improved sketch parameterization with constraints to future work.

We thank the reviewer for this question and we will clarify this and add intermediate visualizations in the updated version of the paper. 

## Error Accumulation

Error accumulation is an inherent challenge in all recent CAD reverse engineering approaches including MiCADangelo. This is due to the fact that a CAD model is typically represented as a sequence that is generated over a number of steps. Recent top-down approaches [15, 9] generate a CAD sequence autoregressively, meaning that inaccurately predicted sequence tokens are fed back into the model, potentially compounding errors and degrading the accuracy of subsequent token predictions. Similarly, bottom-up approaches [8, 18, 7] involve multiple sequential stages, such as per-point segmentation, base or barrel label prediction, and extrusion parameter estimation, with error propagating at each stage. Nevertheless, to assess the robustness of the different steps of MiCADangelo, we evaluate its core stages independently (plane detection, sketch parameterization, and extrusion parameter optimization) in the following tables. In each case, we observe improved performance compared to the corresponding stages in related methods, which explains the superior overall performance achieved by our approach. 

- Plane Detection: We compare MiCADangelo’s plane detection performance against CAD-SIGNet [15], using standard precision, recall, and F1-score. Note that CADSIG-Net is designed to align plane detection with design history, hence its predicted and ground-truth planes are anchored in the original DeepCAD design planes. In contrast, MiCADangelo targets reverse engineering and thus operates on cross-sectional planes obtained by pre-processing DeepCAD (detailed in Appendix A.1). The Table below shows that MiCADangelo achieves strong performance in cross-sectional plane detection, with notably higher metrics than CAD-SIGNet’s performance in the design-plane detection setting.


| **Method** | **Precision** | **Recall** | **F1** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CADSIG-Net [15] | 0.701 | 0.696 | 0.686 |
| Ours | 0.894 | 0.864 | 0.870 |


- Sketch Parameterization: We extend our evaluation on Table 5 of the main paper with the addition of an autoregressive baseline, Vitruvion [4]. We show in the Table below that MiCADangelo outperforms both Vitruvion [4] and Davinci [35] in cross-section parameterization in terms of Sketch Chamfer Distance (SCD).

| **Method** | **SCD** |
| --- | --- |
| Vitruvion [4] | 1.236 |
| Davinci [35] | 0.827 |
| Ours | 0.283 |

- Extrusion Performance: To evaluate extrusion performance, we compare MiCADangelo with Point2Cyl [8], a bottom-up method that estimates extrusion cylinders from 3D point clouds. We use 100 CAD models from the dataset provided in [8] and, for each model, match each ground-truth extrusion cylinder to its closest predicted counterpart from both methods using Chamfer Distance (CD). We then report the average CD across all matched pairs. As shown in the table below, MiCADangelo achieves a lower average CD, indicating more accurate extrusion recovery.
It is worth noting that, due to the high computational cost of Point2Cyl (over 4 hours for 100 samples), this evaluation was limited to 100 models.

| **Method** | **Extrusion CD** |
| --- | --- |
| Point2Cyl [8] | 27.9 |

## Contextual Embeddings 


In Table 4 of the main submission, we ablate the impact of contextual embeddings on plane detection performance. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have extended this analysis to evaluate their effect on the full CAD reconstruction pipeline. The results are presented in the Table below. We observe that contextual embeddings have an effect on the overall CAD reconstruction performance on all reported metrics. 

| **Method** | **Mean CD** | **Median CD** | **IR** | **IoU** | **ECD** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| w/o contextual embeddings | 8.80 | 0.39 | 3.5 | 69.4 | 2.25 |
| w/ contextual embeddings | 2.27 | 0.20 | 2.6 | 80.6 | 0.46 |

Nonetheless, it is interesting to observe that, despite significantly underperforming in cross-section plane detection, our method without contextual embeddings still achieves reasonable overall CAD reconstruction performance. This can be attributed to the robustness of the subsequent stages—sketch parameterization and extrusion optimization—which are capable of recovering plausible reverse engineering design paths, even when the detected cross-section planes deviate from the ground truth. 

As for Invalidity Ratio (IR), we did not observe a drastic drop in performance when omitting the contextual embeddings. This means that a low cross-section plane detection performance does not necessarily imply a high IR. It is important to note that our method achieves an invalidity ratio comparable to CAD‑SIGNet [15] (2.6 for MiCADangelo compared to 0.9 for CAD‑SIGNet on DeepCAD dataset). Invalid outputs are common in recent CAD reconstruction approaches and may arise from various issues (e.g., prediction of self-intersecting sketches). CAD‑SIGNet reduces its invalidity ratio through test‑time sampling (dropping it from 4.4 to 0.9). Our framework could benefit from similar techniques, for example by evaluating intermediate design sequences for validity, which we leave for future work.

We thank the reviewer for the suggestion and we will provide this experiment and discussion along with additional qualitative results as the reviewer suggested in the revised version.


## Choice of N

The value of  $N$ controls the density of cross-section slice sampling, determining the granularity of the input to the reconstruction pipeline. We conduct an ablation on DeepCAD dataset with different $N$ values in the following Table.


| **N** | **Mean CD** | **Median CD** | **IR** | **IoU** | **ECD** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 3.20 | 0.26 | 4.5 | 78.2 | 0.54 |
| 20 | 3.17 | 0.25 | 4.3 | 78.4 | 0.53 |
| 40 | 2.27 | 0.20 | 2.6 | 80.6 | 0.46 |

We observe that larger $N$ values provide the input model with a more dense input representation and slightly increase CAD reconstruction performance across metrics. In this work, we set $N$ to 40, which offers a good balance between accuracy and computational cost. A similar compromise arises in point‑cloud pipelines (as in all competitors [15, 9, 8, 6]), where the input cloud is routinely down‑sampled to a fixed number of points.

## Training Data

All comparison methods are trained on the DeepCAD dataset. The plane detection module of MiCADangelo is likewise trained on DeepCAD. Since the DeepCAD dataset does not include parameterized cross-sections or constraint labels, the sketch parameterization module of MiCADangelo is trained on the SketchGraph dataset of constrained CAD sketches, along with synthetically generated closed loops. Notably, although our sketch parameterization module has not seen DeepCAD cross-sections during training, it generalizes well as demonstrated by the strong CAD reconstruction performance.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
*Strengths*:

1. The paper is clearly structured and well-written. Furthermore, the notation and symbols are clearly defined and explained, making the methodology easy to follow.

2. To my knowledge, the proposed method is novel. The pipeline emulates the workflow of human designers, which is both intuitive and reasonable.

3. The model demonstrates impressive performance. As shown in Figures 3, 4, and 7, the proposed method significantly outperforms baseline methods, particularly on complex models with fine-grained geometric details.

*Weaknesses*:

1. **Effect of Sketch Constraints**: While the authors state that incorporating sketch constraints benefits CAD reconstruction, the mechanism by which this improvement occurs is not sufficiently clear. Although quantitative results are presented in Table 3, additional visualizations or analysis of intermediate steps would help to better demonstrate the practical impact of sketch constraints on the CAD construction process.

2. **Pipeline Complexity and Error Accumulation**: The proposed method comprises four distinct steps, making it notably more complex than end-to-end baselines such as [15]. Since these steps are performed sequentially, there is a risk of error accumulation throughout the pipeline, which is not thoroughly analyzed or discussed.

3. **Role and Impact of Contextual Embeddings**: As indicated in Table 4, contextual embeddings are important for model performance. However, the authors only report the quantitative results of this step. It would be helpful to provide qualitative examples or further analysis of how contextual embeddings affect the quality of reconstructed CAD models. Additionally, the reported precision and recall are below 90%, which is relatively low. Does this limitation explain the model's weaker performance on the IR metric?

summary.value: This paper proposes MiCADangelo, a novel framework for CAD reverse engineering that mimics human design workflows. Given a 3D mesh from a scan, the method selects key cross-sections, infers constrained 2D sketches, and optimizes extrusion parameters to construct a fully parametric and editable CAD model. The method also incorporates CAD sketch constraints into 3D CAD reconstruction. Experiments on DeepCAD and Fusion360 demonstrate significant improvements over prior work in both reconstruction quality and downstream editability.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The framework effectively bridges the gap between 3D scanning and CAD modeling, making it easier for designers to work with scanned data.
- The incorporation of CAD sketch constraints allows for more intuitive and flexible design workflows.
- Experimental results show significant improvements in reconstruction quality and editability compared to prior methods.

Weaknesses:
- The reliance on key cross-sections may limit the framework's ability to capture complex geometries. The performance of the framework on highly detailed or intricate models is not fully explored. For example, the method only handles extrusion-based models, which may not be suitable for all types of CAD designs (such as lofts or sweeps).
- Most parts of the method are rule-based, and the entire pipeline consists of multiple steps that might introduce cumulative errors. It would be interesting to have some high-level schematic comparisons w.r.t. other rule-based methods in terms of pipeline design choices.

questions.value:
- How does the method handle imperfect scans (with holes and mis-oriented normals), or scans with noise? It seems that the proposed stages are mostly sensitive to noise and it would be nice to show how robust the method is towards these issues.
- How does the method perform on more complex geometries with multiple parts and intricate details? It would be interesting to apply the method to a larger mechanics and test the reconstruction quality and editability.

summary.value: This paper proposes a new CAD reverse engineering method, MiCADangelo, that reconstructs fully parametric CAD models from 3D scans. This method addresses the limitations of existing techniques by preserving fine geometric details and incorporating sketch constraints. Specifically, it analyzes 3D scans via 2D cross-sections to identify sketch planes, extracts closed loops into parametric curves, and optimizes extrusions based on local mesh geometry. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing methods in CAD reverse modeling.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. This paper introduces a new and effective method that incorporates sketch-level constraints for CAD reverse engineering to improve the performance.
2. Overall, this paper is well organized, and the proposed method is easy to understand.

Weaknesses:
1. While the method is generally well-explained, some details of the constrained sketch parameterization network and the loss functions are not clear to me. For example, in the second term of the loss function, why do we need to minimize the square of Hi, and what does the subscript i refer to?
2. For the quantitative evaluation, I think the mean Chamfer distance results should be provided, but I only found the median Chamfer distance results.
3. For the evaluation of "Robustness to Real-world Scans", are there any testing results for inputs with noisy or incomplete 3D scans? I think it is common in real scenarios.
4. Since the sketch planes are detected from a set of 2D cross-section slices that are equally sampled along three axes, I wonder how to ensure the desired sketch planes fall in these?
5. As the limitation stated in this paper, this method only supports extrusion, and extrusions are defined based on sketch plane normals, which can be suboptimal for models with non-axis-aligned extrusions.

summary.value: This work approaches parametric CAD reverse engineering, with a particular focus on sketch-extrusion models. The paper introduces a cross-section-based approach for sketch prediction and constraints discovery. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate superior performance compared to prior works, while qualitative results indicate an enhanced capability in handling more complex CAD models than existing approaches.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
+ This work incorporates sketch constraint modeling into 3D CAD reverse engineering, which looks interesting but lacks further constraint optimization.
+ During extrusion optimization, the method jointly optimizes multiple extrusion heights to enhance stability and performance. Experiments (e.g., Fig. 6) demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

Weakness
+ The idea of using cross-section has been explored in several prior works, such as CAD-SIGNet[1], PS-CAD[2], and PlankAssembly[3]. This paper lacks a detailed discussion on how its approach differs from or improves upon these works, raising concerns about the contribution. 
Furthermore, due to the hierarchical and nested nature of CAD construction steps, cross sections cannot fully capture all sketch information. For instance, the sketch of a cut feature may not be visible in the CAD geometry or any extracted cross-section.
+ The modeling of sketch constraints is incremental with a naive network. Similar constraint modeling techniques have been extensively explored in prior works [4, 5] on 2D sketches, and it is uncertain about its novelty. It would be interesting to incorporate sketch constraints for better sketch prediction, but I did not see explicit designs to explore this possiblity. 
+ The paper does not justify the advantages of its differentiable extrusion optimization over prior approaches. Prior works, e.g. Point2Cyl and SECAD-Net, employ an implicit function-based optimization strategy. From a practical standpoint, implicit methods are considered more robust since they can better handle noisy input. Why does this work adopt an explicit optimization formulation?

[1] Khan, Mohammad Sadil, et al. "Cad-signet: Cad language inference from point clouds using layer-wise sketch instance guided attention." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2024.

[2] Yang, Bingchen, et al. "PS-CAD: Local Geometry Guidance via Prompting and Selection for CAD Reconstruction." ACM Transactions on Graphics 44.3 (2025): 1-21.

[3] Hu, Wentao, et al. "Plankassembly: Robust 3d reconstruction from three orthographic views with learnt shape programs." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2023.

[4] Yang, Yuezhi, and Hao Pan. "Discovering design concepts for cad sketches." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 28803-28814.

[5] Seff, Ari, et al. "Vitruvion: A generative model of parametric cad sketches." arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.14124 (2021).

questions.value:
+ Since the plane detection network is trained on DeepCAD dataset, the reviewer is curious about its generality on Fusion360 and CC3D dataset, an evaluation is suggested. 

+ The paper would benefit from a visual result illustrating how a complete reconstruction is decomposed into a set of sketch-extrusions. Such a figure should clearly highlight the intermediate sketches and their corresponding extrusions, including at least one example of a cut extrusion.

limitations.value: The authors have discussed the limitations of orthogonal plane detections. It would be interesting to see discussions about the interference of different extrusions during the optimization process.

final_justification.value: I appreciate the idea of using constraints to improve the CAD modelling pipeline. However, I think the technical contribution, including introducing constraints as an additional prediction task without detailed analysis of the impact of different cases of predicted constraints, is incremental. However, the evaluation of technical contribution is usually subjective; therefore, I downgraded my voting confidence and raised my score.

title.value: MiCADangelo: Fine-Grained Reconstruction of Constrained CAD Models from 3D Scans

abstract.value: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) plays a foundational role in modern manufacturing and product development, often requiring designers to modify or build upon existing models. Converting 3D scans into parametric CAD representations—a process known as CAD reverse engineering—remains a significant challenge due to the high precision and structural complexity of CAD models. Existing deep learning-based approaches typically fall into two categories: bottom-up, geometry-driven methods, which often fail to produce fully parametric outputs, and top-down strategies, which tend to overlook fine-grained geometric details. Moreover, current methods neglect an essential aspect of CAD modeling: sketch-level constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to CAD reverse engineering inspired by how human designers manually perform the task. Our method leverages multi-plane cross-sections to extract 2D patterns and capture fine parametric details more effectively. It enables the reconstruction of detailed and editable CAD models, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and, for the first time, incorporating sketch constraints directly into the reconstruction process.

TLDR.value: We propose a novel CAD reverse engineering method that mimics human design workflows by using multi-plane 2D cross-sections to reconstruct detailed, editable, and fully parametric CAD models.
